title: Picture of a Cat, a Bird, and a Crabapple
medium: Multicolor woodblock print; ink and color on paper

altText: A colorful Chinese woodblock print of a cat, a bird, and a crabapple, as the title says. The picture is made of flat areas of printed ink and color on paper.

context: This multicolor woodblock print was made in Suzhou, in southeast China, sometime between 1662 and 1735 during the Qing dynasty. The Cleveland Museum of Art explains that color woodblock printing flourished in cities such as Suzhou, and that such prints were made with sets of separate blocks, each carved to print one color. Prints like this were sold to hang on walls.

descriptions.k: A cat, a bird, and a crabapple fruit are in this picture. Can you find all three? It was printed with wooden blocks, one for each color. Which animal would you like to meet?
descriptions.g12: This colorful print shows a cat, a bird, and a crabapple. It was made in China long ago with carved wooden blocks. Each block printed one color. Where do you think the cat and bird are looking?
descriptions.g35: Between 1662 and 1735, printers in Suzhou, China, made this color print of a cat, a bird, and a crabapple. They carved a separate wooden block for each color and pressed paper onto each one in turn. Prints like this were sold to hang on walls. What story could connect a cat, a bird, and fruit in one picture?
descriptions.g68: Made in Suzhou during the Qing dynasty, this multicolor woodblock print shows a cat, a bird, and a crabapple. Printers cut one block per color and printed them in careful order, so every color had to line up. Such prints were sold to be hung on walls. How does a picture made in layers of blocks differ from one painted directly with a brush?
descriptions.g910: This Qing-dynasty print from Suzhou (1662-1735) pairs a cat, a bird, and a crabapple. Color woodblock printing required a separate carved block for each color, so the design depended on precise registration and collaboration. As a commercial wall print, it belonged to a market for affordable pictures. How might the technique and the market have shaped what the image looks like?
descriptions.g1112: Produced in Suzhou between 1662 and 1735, this multicolor woodblock print of a cat, a bird, and a crabapple belongs to a commercial printing culture that moved color printing from illustrated books to single-sheet wall pictures. Each color required its own carved block. How does the technique shape the image's flatness and clarity, and how might its status as a mass-produced picture complicate usual ideas about fine art?

k.daily: Where is the cat? Where is the bird? Point to each one.
k.emotion: Does the cat look sleepy or watchful to you? What shows it?
k.observation: Find the crabapple. What color is it?
k.analysis: What do you think the cat and the bird might do next?
k.line: Trace the edge of the cat with your finger. Is the line thick or thin?
k.shape: What shapes do you see in the bird and the fruit?
k.color: Which color do you notice first? Why?
k.texture: This was printed, not painted. Does the paper look smooth or rough?
k.space: Which one is closest to you, and which is farther away?
k.light: Is this picture bright or soft? How can you tell?
k.meaning: Why might someone hang a picture of animals on their wall?
k.culture: Long ago, people in China hung prints in their homes. What do you hang in yours?
k.technique: Each color came from a different block. How could you make a print with a potato?
k.personal: If you made your own animal picture, who would be in it?
k.critical: Would you change anything about where the cat and bird are? Why?

g12.daily: Which part of the picture shows the cat, and which shows the bird?
g12.emotion: Does the picture feel peaceful or full of action? Point to what makes you feel that.
g12.observation: List what you see, from the biggest thing to the smallest.
g12.analysis: Why does your eye go to the cat first, or does it go somewhere else?
g12.line: Follow the outlines. Are the lines smooth, or do they have sharp turns?
g12.shape: How do round shapes, like fruit, mix with long shapes, like branches or a tail?
g12.color: How do the colors make the animals stand out from the paper?
g12.texture: How do the printed lines make fur and feathers look different?
g12.space: How does the print show that some things are near and some are far?
g12.light: Does this picture use shadows, or mostly flat color? How can you tell?
g12.meaning: Why might the artist put a cat, a bird, and fruit together?
g12.culture: What might a print like this tell us about everyday life in old China?
g12.technique: Each color needed its own block. Why would a printer plan carefully?
g12.personal: How would you arrange animals and fruit so a picture feels lively?
g12.critical: Is a printed picture as special as a painted one? Use details to explain.

g35.daily: Which part of the picture surprises you, and what in it makes you say so?
g35.emotion: How would you describe the mood of the cat and the bird, and what choices create it?
g35.observation: Look carefully at where the cat and bird are placed. What relationship do you see between them?
g35.analysis: How does the artist arrange the cat, bird, and crabapple so your eye moves around?
g35.line: How do the outlines in this print differ from the lines in a brush painting?
g35.shape: How do the shapes of animals and fruit fit together on the page?
g35.color: How do the printed colors work together, and where are they strongest?
g35.texture: Prints can show texture in flat color. How does this one suggest fur, feathers, or leaves?
g35.space: How does the artist show space on a flat sheet of paper?
g35.light: How does the print show light, if at all, without using shading?
g35.meaning: Cats and birds appear together in many stories. What could this combination suggest?
g35.culture: Why might a household in the Qing dynasty have wanted a print like this?
g35.technique: Why would carving a separate block for every color take careful planning?
g35.personal: What animals would you pair in a picture, and what would you want viewers to think?
g35.critical: Some people value paintings more than prints. What would you say about this one?

g68.daily: Which detail in the print do you notice only after looking for a while?
g68.emotion: What mood do the cat's and bird's positions create, and how does the picture build tension or calm?
g68.observation: Describe how the three subjects are placed on the sheet. What is the focal point?
g68.analysis: How do printed outlines and flat areas of color guide your eye across the picture?
g68.line: How does the print use line to describe form without the soft shading of a painting?
g68.shape: How do the cat, bird, and fruit fit together as a balanced arrangement of shapes?
g68.color: How might the printers have chosen and limited their colors, and what effect does that have?
g68.texture: How does a woodblock print suggest texture differently from a painted surface?
g68.space: How does the picture create depth with so little shading?
g68.light: What does the lack of strong cast shadows tell you about this tradition of image-making?
g68.meaning: What symbolic meanings might viewers in China have connected with a cat, a bird, and a fruit? What would you need to know to be sure?
g68.culture: How does a mass-produced wall print show something about city life and markets in the Qing dynasty?
g68.technique: How does the need to line up several blocks shape what is possible in the design?
g68.personal: What would you want to learn about the printers and the people who bought this?
g68.critical: Does the technique of printing make this image less original, or does it make it a different kind of art? Argue a side.

g910.daily: What small detail in the cat or bird changes how you read the whole picture?
g910.emotion: How does the picture suggest a relationship between predator and prey without becoming threatening?
g910.observation: Study how the three subjects occupy the page. What hierarchy of attention does the composition create?
g910.analysis: Analyze how the designer balances the cat's mass against the bird and the fruit.
g910.line: How do outline and color blocks work together, compared with a brush painting's variable line?
g910.shape: How does the simplification of forms in a carved-block print affect how animals are recognized?
g910.color: How does the restricted palette of separate printed colors shape the picture's mood and clarity?
g910.texture: What does the printed surface suggest about the relationship between carved wood and the image it leaves on paper?
g910.space: How does the print organize space on a flat sheet without relying on linear perspective?
g910.light: How might the absence of dramatic shading connect to the aims of this tradition?
g910.meaning: Without claiming a single meaning, what associations might a cat, a bird, and a crabapple have carried for viewers of that time?
g910.culture: How does a commercial wall print reveal the growth of a visual culture beyond the court and the elite?
g910.technique: How did producing a design in layers of carved blocks require collaboration between designer, carver, and printer?
g910.personal: What does this print make you question about the line between decoration, commerce, and art?
g910.critical: Should handmade prints in editions be judged on the same terms as unique paintings? Support your answer.

g1112.daily: Which compositional choice in this print most resists a purely decorative reading?
g1112.emotion: How might the cat-and-bird pairing hold both charm and tension for different viewers?
g1112.observation: Analyze the hierarchy of attention among the three subjects and what it implies about the image's purpose.
g1112.analysis: How do the carved outline and printed color fields establish a different visual logic from brush painting?
g1112.line: How do the stylized forms interact with the idea of observation from nature?
g1112.shape: How does the picture reconcile naturalistic subjects with the geometry of the page?
g1112.color: Evaluate how the separate printed colors build unity and emphasis within a limited set of blocks.
g1112.texture: What does the print's surface reveal about the relationship between carving, ink, and paper?
g1112.space: How does the print create pictorial space without Western-style illusionism, and with what consequences?
g1112.light: How might the absence of cast shadows reflect conventions about what a picture should record?
g1112.meaning: What interpretive risks arise when we assign fixed symbolic meanings to a cat, a bird, and a crabapple?
g1112.culture: How does this print reflect the commercial expansion of color printing in Jiangnan cities, and what does that reveal about audience and taste?
g1112.technique: How does the multi-block process complicate ideas of individual authorship and the 'hand' of the artist?
g1112.personal: How does this work challenge a hierarchy that places unique paintings above multiple prints?
g1112.critical: What criteria would you use to argue for this print's significance to someone who sees it as ordinary decoration?

teacherNote.context: A multicolor woodblock print made in Suzhou, China, between 1662 and 1735 in the Qing dynasty. The museum notes that color printing flourished in Jiangnan cities and that each color was printed from a separate carved block. No maker's name is recorded.
directions: Have students make a simple two-color potato or foam print, noticing how each color needs its own printing step.
Ask students to imagine the story between the cat and the bird, then discuss how the artist hints at it without words.
Discuss why a household might buy an affordable print and how that differs from owning a one-of-a-kind painting.
